a: Isaac was weaned
p: Chapter 17 retells Genesis 21:8-21, the weaning of Isaac and the sending away of Hagar.
b: Genesis says: "The child grew and was weaned, and on the day Isaac was weaned Abraham held a great feast" (Genesis 21:8). Jubilees keeps the feast and adds a date: the first year of the fifth week, in the third month. Charles thought "fifth" was a slip for "fourth", as in 16:15; VanderKam's Ge'ez text reads "fifth" (ḫams), and the Plain English Translation follows it.

a: fifth week of this jubilee
p: A "week" here is seven years, and a jubilee is forty-nine years: the book dates every event this way.
b: Jubilees counts history in jubilees of forty-nine years (seven times seven), each split into seven "weeks" of seven years. So "the first year of the fifth week of this jubilee" means year 29 of that jubilee. The book never gives a year counted from creation; Charles's margin dates ("2003 A.M.") are his own sums, not the text. See the jubilee note in chapter 1 and the jubilee topic.
orig: ዘሱባዔ ኃምስ ኀደገ ጥበ ይስሐቅ በዝንቱ ኢዮቤልዉ (zäsubaʿe ḫams ḫädägä ṭəbä yəsḥäq bäznətu ʾiyobelwu)

a: had not died childless
p: Abraham had feared dying without children (Genesis 15:2-3). Now he sees sons of his own.
b: In Genesis, Abram's first complaint to God is that he has no child and a servant will inherit (Genesis 15:2-3). Jubilees closes that thread here, with both sons standing before him. Charles points back to 16:16, where the angels promised that Abraham would see six more sons before he died.

a: the day Lot parted from him
p: After Lot left, God promised Abraham offspring like the dust of the earth (Genesis 13:14-17).
b: Genesis places the great land promise right after Lot chose the Jordan plain: "If anyone could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted too" (Genesis 13:16). Jubilees retold that scene in 13:19-21. Abraham now sees the first sign that the promise is coming true.

a: playing and dancing
p: Genesis has Ishmael "laughing"; Jubilees has him "playing and dancing", and Abraham happily watching.
b: Hebrew Genesis 21:9 has one word, metsaḥeq, which the site renders "laughing"; it is the same root as Isaac's name. Interpreters have long asked what was wrong with it: mockery, play, or worse. Jubilees removes the blame. Ishmael is only playing and dancing, and Abraham rejoices. Sarah's jealousy is the only cause. Charles notes that the Latin reads "with Isaac" here (cum Isac), as the Septuagint of Genesis does, and suspects the Ge'ez word for "dancing" (wäyzäfn) is a corruption of that phrase. See the variant.

a: she became jealous of Ishmael
t: Compared with the Bible: Sarah's motive
p: Genesis gives no motive for Sarah's demand. Jubilees names one: jealousy.
b: Genesis states only what Sarah saw and what she said (Genesis 21:9-10). Jubilees adds "she became jealous" (wäqänʾät). This goes beyond the Bible. It makes Ishmael blameless and Sarah's demand a human feeling, yet God still tells Abraham to do what she says (17:6). The book cares more about the line through Isaac than about clearing Sarah.

a: listen to her words and do it
p: God's answer is Genesis 21:12 almost word for word, with "and do it" added.
b: Compare the site's Genesis: "Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her, for it is through Isaac that offspring will be named for you" (Genesis 21:12). Jubilees adds "a name" to "offspring", as it does again in 19:16. Paul quotes the same line in Romans 9:7, and Hebrews 11:18 quotes it about the binding of Isaac.

a: I will make him a great nation
p: Genesis 21:13 in Hebrew says only "a nation"; Jubilees says "a great nation", as other old versions do.
b: The Ge'ez has "into a great people" (wəstä ʿäbiy ḥəzb). Charles notes that "great" is found in the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Vulgate of Genesis 21:13, but not in the Hebrew Masoretic text or Onkelos. It is one of many places where Jubilees agrees with a Bible text other than the one behind most English Bibles.

a: put them on the shoulders of Hagar and the boy
p: By Genesis's own numbers Ishmael was a teenager, which makes "the boy" on the shoulder a puzzle.
b: Genesis 16:16 and Genesis 21:5 make Ishmael about fourteen when Isaac is born, and older at his weaning. Yet in Genesis 21:14-15 Hagar carries and then "casts" the boy. Jubilees keeps the picture and puts the load on both their shoulders. It never stops to solve the problem, but it does call Ishmael "the boy" (ḥəḍan, a child) throughout, as Genesis does.

a: an olive tree
p: Genesis has "one of the bushes". The Ge'ez borrows a Greek word for "olive".
b: Where Genesis 21:15 has a desert bush, Jubilees has ʾelyas. Charles explains that this is the Greek elaia, "olive", while the Septuagint of Genesis has elatē, "fir". Either way the word passed through Greek, which shows the Ge'ez was translated from a Greek version and not straight from Hebrew.

a: one of the holy ones
t: An angel, "one of the holy ones"
p: Jubilees explains "the angel of God" in Genesis 21:17 as one of the holy angels.
b: The Ge'ez has mälʾäk ʾämlak ʾäḥädu ʾəmqədusan, "an angel of God, one of the holy ones". In Genesis it is God who hears the boy's voice; in Jubilees the Lord hears Hagar's voice and sees the boy. Charles notes that "she opened her eyes" in 17:12 is unexpected, since Genesis 21:19 has God open them.
orig: መልአክ አምላክ አሐዱ እምቅዱሳን (mälʾäk ʾämlak ʾäḥädu ʾəmqədusan)

a: Nebaioth
p: Ishmael's firstborn, from Genesis 25:13. His mother's words seem to play on his name.
b: Genesis lists Nebaioth as "Ishmael's firstborn" (Genesis 25:13). The Ge'ez spells the name nabewot. Hagar's reason, "The Lord was near me when I called on him", probably played on the name in Hebrew. Charles says we would expect the Hebrew word behind "was near" to share some letters with "Nebaioth"; the Ge'ez cannot show it. Who names the child is unclear: the Ge'ez says "she" (the mother) and then "he called".

a: there were voices in heaven about Abraham
t: Compared with the Bible: why the test?
p: Genesis 22:1 says only "God put Abraham to the test." Jubilees opens a scene in heaven first.
b: Genesis gives no reason for the test. Jubilees supplies one, shaped like the opening of Job: voices in heaven praise Abraham, an accuser answers, and the test follows (Job 1:6-12). This goes beyond the Bible. It also shifts who wants the test: in Genesis God tests Abraham (Genesis 22:1); in Jubilees God allows a test that Mastema proposes. The book still keeps God in charge, since the Lord already knows Abraham is faithful (17:17).

a: on the twelfth of that month
p: The test begins on the 12th of the first month. Charles worked out that Isaac would be twenty-three.
b: Charles notes that by the book's dates Isaac is about twenty-three when he is offered, and that the rabbinic chronicle Seder Olam makes him thirty-seven. He also points to 16:12 and 17:15. Fitzmyer counts the three days of 18:3 from this date and reaches the fifteenth of the first month, "when Passover was being celebrated"; see the chapter page for 18.

a: Prince Mastema
p: The chief of the evil spirits, here in the role of the accuser in Job. His title is debated.
b: The Ge'ez is mäkʷännä mästema, "Prince Mastema" (VanderKam's text, here and at 18:9, 12). Charles printed "the prince of the Mastema" from two of his manuscripts. Fitzmyer notes the same question in the Hebrew of a Qumran text, 4Q225, whose first editors, VanderKam and Milik, read "the Prince of the Mastemah", where others read a name; he explains the word as meaning judicial "opposition", like the accuser in Job 1. For Mastema's first appearance and the spirits under him, see 10:8.

a: Tell him to offer him up as a burnt offering on the altar
t: Satan before God, in the rabbis
p: The Talmud tells a similar story: Satan speaks before God, and the test of Abraham follows.
b: Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 89b reads "after these things" in Genesis 22:1 as "after the words of Satan": Satan says before the Holy One that Abraham has never offered him anything from his feasts, and God answers that Abraham would sacrifice even his son if told. Charles quotes the passage beside this verse. In both, the accuser's charge sets the test in motion. The rabbis may not have known Jubilees; the shared shape may come from reading Genesis 22 beside Job 1.

a: He had tested him with his land and with famine
p: Jewish tradition counts ten trials of Abraham. Jubilees numbers only the tenth (19:8); the full count is Charles's.
b: The Mishnah says: "With ten trials was Abraham our father tried, and he withstood them all" (Mishnah Avot 5:3). It does not list them. Jubilees names: leaving his land, famine, the wealth of kings, his wife taken, circumcision, Ishmael and Hagar sent away (17:17). Charles counts these as seven, taking the sending away of Ishmael and of Hagar as two trials, the sixth and seventh. He adds Sarah's barrenness and the binding of Isaac as the eighth and ninth, which he says are "not specifically reckoned as such in our text". The text itself numbers only Sarah's burial, "the tenth trial" (19:3, 8). He compares the later lists of Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer and Maimonides, and notes that two medieval writers also make Sarah's burial the tenth.

a: the wealth of kings
p: Probably the spoils Abraham refused from the king of Sodom (Genesis 14:21-24; Jubilees 13:28-29).
b: Most of the trials are hardships. This one is an offer: after the war of the kings, Abraham would not take "a thread or a sandal strap" from the king of Sodom (Genesis 14:23). It may also include the gifts of Pharaoh (Genesis 12:16). Jubilees treats wealth as a test of faith, as much as famine.

a: His soul did not lose patience
p: Two marks of Abraham's faith: he did not lose patience, and he did not delay obeying.
b: The Ge'ez says his soul "was not impatient" (ʾitäʾäntälä näfsu) and he "did not delay doing" (ʾigʷändäyä gäbiroto). Patience returns as the word for the tenth trial (19:3, 8). The point is that Abraham trusted without complaint and obeyed at once, as Genesis shows by "Abraham got up early in the morning" (Genesis 22:3).
orig: ወኢተአንተለ ነፍሱ ወኢጐንደየ ገቢሮቶ (wäʾitäʾäntälä näfsu wäʾigʷändäyä gäbiroto)

a: The Lord said to him
t: Compared with the Bible: who gives the command?
p: In Genesis "God" (Elohim) speaks; in Jubilees it is the Lord, and the angel tells the story.
b: Genesis 22 begins with God (Elohim) and turns to "the angel of the LORD" at 22:11. Jubilees, told by the angel of the presence, follows that shape: the Lord commands (18:1-2), then the angel calls from heaven (18:10-11) and speaks again in the Lord's name (18:14). The Ge'ez always uses ʾƎgziʾabḥer, "the Lord", since Ge'ez has no separate divine name.

a: your beloved son, the one you love
p: Hebrew Genesis 22:2 says "your only one"; Jubilees says "your beloved", as the Septuagint does.
b: The Ge'ez fəquräkä zätafäqr is "your beloved whom you love". Charles notes that this agrees with the Septuagint's agapētos ("beloved") against the Hebrew yaḥid, "only one". The same Greek word is used of Jesus at his baptism, where the site renders it "my dearly loved Son" (Mark 1:11). In 18:11 and 18:15 the Ge'ez has "your firstborn" instead. See the variant at 18:15.

a: the high land
p: Genesis names "the land of Moriah". Jubilees says "the high land", as the Greek of Genesis does.
b: The Ge'ez has mədär ləʿlət, "high land". Charles notes that this matches the Septuagint of Genesis 22:2, "the high land" (tēn gēn tēn hypsēlēn), against the Hebrew "land of Moriah", and that two of his manuscripts read "mountain". Jubilees does not lose the place, though: in 18:13 it names the mountain as Zion. 2 Chronicles 3:1 already puts Solomon's Temple "on Mount Moriah".

a: He came to a well of water
t: Compared with the Bible: a well
p: Genesis has no well here. Jubilees adds one where Abraham leaves his servants.
b: In Genesis, Abraham sees the place far off and speaks to his servants (Genesis 22:4-5). Jubilees adds that he came to a well. Wells mark the Abraham and Isaac stories (Beersheba, the Well of the Oath, 18:17), and Hagar's rescue came at a well (17:12). The detail goes beyond Genesis but does not change it.

a: we will come back to you
p: Abraham says "we" will come back. Readers have long asked what he expected.
b: The Ge'ez, like Genesis 22:5, has the plural, nəgäbʾ, "we will return". Hebrews 11:19 reads it as faith in resurrection: "He reckoned that God could raise people even from the dead." It can also be read as a father hiding the truth from his son and servants. Jubilees does not explain it, but its frame (Abraham is already known to be faithful, 17:17) fits a hopeful reading.

a: laid it on his son Isaac
p: As in Genesis 22:6. Early Christians saw in it Christ carrying his cross.
b: The scene is Genesis 22:6, kept close to word for word. Many church fathers compared Isaac carrying the wood with Jesus carrying his cross (John 19:17). Jubilees has no such interest; its focus is on Abraham's faithfulness and Mastema's defeat. See the akedah topic for the Christian and Jewish readings.

a: Here are the fire, the knife and the wood
p: Isaac names three things here, not two: Jubilees adds the knife.
b: In Genesis 22:7 Isaac says, "Here are the fire and the wood." Jubilees has nahu ʾəsat wämäṭbaḥt wäʿḍäw, "here are the fire, the knife and the wood", and Isaac ends with "Father". The knife makes Isaac's question sharper: he sees everything needed to kill, except an animal.
orig: ናሁ እሳት ወመጥባሕት ወዕፀው (nahu ʾəsat wämäṭbaḥt wäʿḍäw)

a: the mountain of the Lord
p: Genesis 22:9 says only "the place God had told him about". Jubilees already names it.
b: The phrase points ahead to 18:13 (Mount Zion) and to Genesis 22:14, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be seen." Isaiah 2:3 uses "the mountain of the LORD" for the Temple mount. Charles notes the difference from Genesis 22:9.

a: I was standing in front of him and in front of Prince Mastema
t: Compared with the Bible: the watching angels
p: The angel who tells the story was there, with Mastema watching. Genesis has neither.
b: The narrator, the angel of the presence, stands between Abraham and Mastema, and the Lord sends him to stop the knife. This goes beyond Genesis, where the angel of the LORD simply calls from heaven (Genesis 22:11). A Qumran text, 4Q225 (called Pseudo-Jubilees), tells the scene with more figures: Fitzmyer's translation has "holy angels" standing and weeping, the angels of Mastemah rejoicing and saying "Now he will perish", and Isaac asking his father to bind him. Jubilees has none of these.

a: I know that he fears the Lord
p: The Ge'ez verb can mean "I know". The Latin version, at 18:11, has "I have shown".
b: The Ge'ez ʾäʾmärku is "I have known, I know", like Hebrew yada'ti in Genesis 22:12, "Now I know that you fear God." At 18:11 the Latin version has manifestavi, "I have shown", and Charles prefers it in both verses: the test proves Abraham's faith to Mastema and to everyone (18:16, "I have made it known to all"). The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. See the variant at 18:11.

a: He was terrified
p: Only Jubilees says Abraham was terrified when the angel called.
b: The Ge'ez wädängäḍä means "and he was startled, terrified". Genesis 22:11 says only that he answered, "Here I am." The word adds a human moment at the edge of the knife.

a: your son, your firstborn
p: Genesis 22:12 says "your only one". Here the Ge'ez has "your firstborn".
b: The Ge'ez wäldäkä bäkʷräkä is "your son, your firstborn". Isaac was not Abraham's firstborn by birth; Ishmael was. But in this book Isaac holds the firstborn's place (compare 19:29, where Jacob too is to be God's "firstborn son"). Hebrews 11:17 keeps the idea of "only" with the Greek monogenēs, "his only son".

a: Prince Mastema was put to shame
p: The test was Mastema's idea, and it ends with his defeat, not with Abraham's.
b: Jubilees adds one line to Genesis 22:13: Mastema "was put to shame" (wätäḫäfrä). The story becomes a contest won by Abraham's faithfulness, as Job's patience answers the accuser in Job 1-2. In Fitzmyer's translation of the Qumran text 4Q225, fragment 2, a broken line begins "The prince Mastemah bound". In Jubilees, Mastema's shame here is the first of his defeats; at 48:12 he is "not put to shame" by the plagues, and at 48:15 he is bound so Israel can leave Egypt.

a: It is Mount Zion
t: Compared with the Bible: Moriah is Zion
p: Jubilees names the mountain of the binding as Mount Zion, the Temple mount.
b: Genesis does not say where "the land of Moriah" is. 2 Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon built the Temple "on Mount Moriah". Jubilees goes further and calls the place of the binding Mount Zion. This agrees with the direction of 2 Chronicles but goes beyond Genesis. For Jubilees, the offering of Isaac and the Temple's sacrifices belong to the same mountain.

a: The Lord Has Seen
p: Genesis 22:14 plays on "see" and "be seen". The Ge'ez keeps only "has seen".
b: The Ge'ez has ʾəgziʾäbḥer rəʾyä, "the Lord has seen", twice. Hebrew Genesis 22:14 names the place "The LORD Will See" and then says "it will be seen" (or "he will be seen") on the mountain. Charles notes that the Latin of Jubilees here has "was seen" (visus est), passive like the Hebrew and the Septuagint. See the variant.

a: just as we appeared in order to speak to him in the name of the Lord
t: Angels speaking in the Lord's name
p: The narrator explains Genesis's "angel of the LORD": the Lord spoke through the angels.
b: In Genesis 22:15-16 the angel calls a second time but speaks as God: "By myself I swear, says the LORD." Jubilees explains how: the angels appeared and spoke in the Lord's name. VanderKam's text has ʾästärʾäynä, "we appeared". Charles prints "he caused us to appear" from one manuscript and notes that another has "we appeared". This is close to the New Testament idea that the law was given "through angels" (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2).

a: the cities of their enemies
p: Genesis 22:17 has "the gate of his enemies"; Jubilees has "cities", as several old versions do.
b: The Ge'ez has ʾähgurä ḍäromu, "the cities of their enemies". Charles notes that "cities" is also in the Samaritan version, the Septuagint, the Syriac and Onkelos of Genesis 22:17, while the Hebrew and the Vulgate have "gate". The site's Genesis reads "the gate of his enemies". A city gate stood for the whole city, so the sense is the same.

a: I have made it known to all that you are faithful to me
t: Compared with the Bible: the test made public
p: Jubilees adds why the test was needed: to show everyone, not to tell God, that Abraham was faithful.
b: Genesis 22:12 says, "Now I know that you fear God." That line has troubled readers: did God not know before? Jubilees answers by its frame. The Lord knew already (17:17); the test was for Mastema and for all (18:16). This goes beyond Genesis but fits it. James 2:21-23 makes a related point: Abraham's act showed his faith at work.

a: the Well of the Oath
t: Beersheba, the Well of the Oath
p: Jubilees translates the name Beersheba: "the well of the oath".
b: The Ge'ez ʿäzäqtä mäḥäla means "the well of the oath", a rendering of the Hebrew name Beersheba, explained in Genesis 21:31 and Genesis 26:33. Jubilees uses both forms in one verse, the name and its meaning. Genesis 22:19 ends the story the same way: "Abraham lived at Beersheba."

a: He named it the festival of the Lord
p: Abraham keeps a seven-day feast every year to remember the journey. The book does not name it.
b: The feast lasts seven days, "after the seven days in which he went and came back". Jubilees never says which later feast this is. Fitzmyer notes that the dates in 17:15 and 18:3 bring Abraham to the mountain on the fifteenth of the first month, "when Passover was being celebrated", and judges that the book makes the link "only indirectly". The Feast of Unleavened Bread begins on the fifteenth and lasts seven days (Leviticus 23:6). See the chapter page.

a: written on the heavenly tablets
t: A law on the heavenly tablets
p: As often in Jubilees, a custom of the patriarchs becomes a law already written in heaven.
b: The book often ends a story this way: what Abraham did is "ordained and written on the heavenly tablets" for Israel. Here the law is to keep the seven-day festival "with festival joy" (the Latin has in laetitia gaudentes, "rejoicing in gladness", Charles notes). See 3:10 on the heavenly tablets, and the heavenly-tablets topic.

a: across from Hebron, that is, Kiriath-arba
p: Genesis 23:2 gives Hebron its older name, Kiriath-arba. Jubilees uses both.
b: The Ge'ez spells it qäriyatarbaq. The site's Genesis says Sarah "died at Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron" (Genesis 23:2). Charles notes the Septuagint's "in the city of Arbok". "Two weeks of years" is fourteen years.

a: In the first year of the third week of this jubilee
t: A date that does not fit
p: Charles thought "third" should be "second", so that Isaac marries at forty after Sarah dies.
b: Genesis 25:20 says Isaac married Rebekah at forty, and Jubilees places the wedding in "the fourth year" (19:10). Charles argued that the numbers only work if Sarah died in the second week, not the third. VanderKam's Ge'ez text reads "third" (śals), and the Plain English Translation keeps it. The book's dates are not always consistent; Charles marks several as corrupt (17:1; 20:1; 21:1; 22:1).

a: We tested him
t: Compared with the Bible: Sarah's burial as a test
p: Here the angels test Abraham, not Mastema. Genesis does not call the burial a test.
b: Genesis 23 tells the purchase of the cave as a careful deal. Jubilees reads it as a trial: would Abraham, who had been promised the whole land, complain that he had to beg and pay for a grave in it (19:9)? He did not. This goes beyond Genesis. The tester here is "we", the angels of the presence.

a: the double cave
p: Jubilees, like the Septuagint, translates Machpelah as "the double cave".
b: The Ge'ez bäʿät zäkaʿbät means "the cave that is double". Charles notes that it matches the Septuagint's to spēlaion to diploun for Hebrew "the cave of Machpelah", which may mean "double". The cave is shown today in Hebron as the Cave of the Patriarchs.

a: for forty pieces of silver
p: The Ge'ez says forty; Genesis and the Latin of Jubilees say four hundred. See the variant.
b: The Ge'ez bäʾärbəʿa bərur is "for forty silver". Genesis 23:15-16 has four hundred shekels, and Charles reports that the Latin version of Jubilees agrees with Genesis. He judged the Ge'ez wrong. In Ge'ez the words for "forty" (ʾärbəʿa) and "four hundred" are different, so either a copyist slipped or a number word was lost.

a: He bowed down to them twice
p: Genesis 23:7 and Genesis 23:12 show Abraham bowing twice to the people of the land.
b: Jubilees sums up the long bargaining scene of Genesis 23 in two verses and keeps two details: Abraham refused the gift and paid in full, and he bowed twice (Genesis 23:7; Genesis 23:12). Paying the full price made the grave his own beyond any later claim.

a: two jubilees, four weeks of years and one year
p: A hundred and twenty-seven years is 98 + 28 + 1: two jubilees, four weeks and a year.
b: The book turns Genesis 23:1 into its own counting: two jubilees (98 years), four weeks of years (28) and one year. Charles notes that one manuscript and the Latin leave out "of the years" in the last line.

a: This is the tenth trial
p: Jubilees makes Sarah's burial the tenth trial. Most rabbinic lists end with the binding of Isaac.
b: The Mishnah knows of ten trials but does not list them (Mishnah Avot 5:3). Charles sets out later lists: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer ends with the offering of Isaac, while Jonah Girondi and Simon Duran, like Jubilees, end with the burial of Sarah. Ending with a burial makes a point: the hardest test was not a dramatic sacrifice but a quiet humiliation, paying for a grave in a land God had promised him (19:9).

a: about the promise of the land
p: Charles translated "the rumour in the land". The Ge'ez can mean the word spoken about the land.
b: The Ge'ez is nəbab zämdər, literally "the speech of the land". Charles took it as "the rumour in the land", what people said. The next words explain it, though: "that the Lord had said he would give it to him". So the Plain English Translation reads it as the promise about the land. Either way, Abraham did not use God's promise as a claim against the sons of Heth.

a: the friend of the Lord
p: Jubilees is among the oldest books to call Abraham "friend of God", as James 2:23 later does.
b: The Ge'ez ʿärkä ʾəgziʾäbḥer is "friend of the Lord". The title grows from 2 Chronicles 20:7, "your friend Abraham", and Isaiah 41:8, where the site renders "offspring of Abraham, who loved me" (Hebrew ʾohavi, "my lover, my friend"). James 2:23 says he "was called the friend of God". Charles also cites Philo and 1 Clement 10:1. Jubilees adds that the name was written on the heavenly tablets because he "was found faithful", which comes near James's link between faith shown in deeds and friendship with God.

a: Bethuel, who fathered the Bethuelites
p: The Ge'ez line on Rebekah's family is muddled; Charles corrected it from the Latin.
b: Genesis 24:15 makes Rebekah "the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham's brother Nahor". The Ge'ez repeats part of the line and has a puzzling phrase, wälädomu läbatuʾelawiyan, "he fathered them, the Bethuelites". Charles treated the first "daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, brother of Abraham" as a copying repeat already in the Greek (the Latin has it too) and corrected the rest with the Latin. See the variant.

a: a third wife
t: Compared with the Bible: who was Keturah?
p: Genesis says only that Abraham took another wife, Keturah. Jubilees says she was a household servant's child.
b: Genesis 25:1 names Keturah without background, and 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her a concubine. Jubilees makes her his third wife, from the families of his servants, and explains why he did not take Hagar back: Hagar had died. Charles notes that later Jewish tradition (Genesis Rabbah 61 and the Targums) solved it the other way, by making Keturah Hagar under a new name, a view Jerome also reports. This goes beyond the Bible.

a: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah
p: The names of Genesis 25:2, given in their Genesis forms. The Ge'ez spells them differently.
b: The Ge'ez has zänbär, yaksən, maday, madan, ʾiyazboq and sehiya. The Plain English Translation uses the Genesis forms (Genesis 25:2). Midian's line will matter later: Moses' father-in-law was a priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16).

a: Jacob was blameless and upright
p: Genesis 25:27 calls Jacob tam, "quiet" in the site. Jubilees has "complete and upright".
b: The Ge'ez fəṣum wäratʿ is "complete (perfect) and upright". The Hebrew tam in Genesis 25:27 is the word used of Job, "blameless" (Job 1:1), but in Jacob's case most English Bibles take it as "quiet" or "plain". Charles's manuscripts read "smooth and upright", which he thought combined two Greek renderings of tam, or drew on Genesis 27:11, where Jacob is "smooth". Jubilees leaves no doubt that Jacob was a good man.

a: Jacob learned to write
t: Compared with the Bible: Jacob the scholar
p: Jubilees adds that Jacob learned to write, and Esau learned war.
b: Genesis says Esau was a hunter and Jacob "stayed among the tents" (Genesis 25:27). Jubilees turns the tents into a school: Jacob learned letters (mäṣḥäf, writing, books). Charles notes that the Targums later have Jacob study in the school of Shem and Eber. Writing matters in this book: Enoch was the first to learn it (4:17), and Jacob's books go to Levi (45:16).

a: Abraham loved Jacob, but Isaac loved Esau
t: Compared with the Bible: Abraham sees Jacob grow up
p: In Genesis, Abraham dies when the twins are fifteen and never meets them in the story. Jubilees has him choose Jacob.
b: By Genesis's numbers Abraham was alive until Jacob and Esau were fifteen (Genesis 21:5; Genesis 25:7; Genesis 25:26), but Genesis never puts them together. Jubilees fills the gap with a whole relationship: Abraham loves Jacob, blesses him (19:26-29; 22:10-30) and dies with him in his arms (23:1-3). Genesis 25:28 says "Isaac loved Esau... but Rebekah loved Jacob"; Jubilees adds Abraham to Rebekah's side.

a: it was through Jacob that a name and offspring would be named for him
p: The words of Genesis 21:12 about Isaac are now applied to Jacob.
b: In 17:6 the Lord told Abraham, "it is through Isaac that a name and offspring will be named for you." Abraham now sees that the same line runs through Jacob, not Esau. Charles notes that Abraham recognizes by Esau's conduct the one chosen beforehand (compare 2:20). Paul makes a similar choosing argument in Romans 9:7-13.

a: a people of his own
p: Charles says the line is drawn "word for word" from Deuteronomy 7:6.
b: Compare: "The LORD your God has chosen you out of all the peoples on the face of the ground to be his people, his own private treasure" (Deuteronomy 7:6). Charles adds that the Ethiopic translators of the Bible regularly mistranslated the Greek periousios, "special possession", which is why the Ge'ez reads oddly here (läḥzəb qawm).

a: Let your hands be strong
p: Abraham charges Rebekah, not Isaac, to guard the promised line.
b: Abraham's words put Rebekah in charge of Jacob's future. That prepares for her part in Genesis 27, where she helps Jacob take Isaac's blessing. In Jubilees her action carries out Abraham's wish, which softens the deceit (see chapter 26). "Strong hands" is a common Hebrew picture for courage (2 Samuel 2:7).

a: If anyone can count the sand of the earth
t: Like the dust of the earth
p: From Genesis 13:16, with "sand" for "dust".
b: The site's Genesis reads: "If anyone could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted too" (Genesis 13:16). Jubilees has "sand" (ḫoḍa). Charles points out the contrast with Jubilees 13:20, which retold the same promise with "dust".

a: Shem, Noah, Enoch, Mahalalel, Enosh, Seth and Adam
p: The list leaves out Methuselah and other fathers, and names Mahalalel, about whom the Bible says little.
b: Charles calls the list "peculiar for its omissions and its insertions". Nothing special is known of Mahalalel (Genesis 5:12-17), and Methuselah, Lamech, Jared and Kenan are missing. He also notes that the rabbis were divided about Adam, some counting him a saint. Jubilees treats Adam as righteous: he offered incense on the day he left Eden (3:27).

a: to lay the foundations of heaven
t: Jacob's line and the new creation
p: Israel's line will share in God's renewal of heaven and earth.
b: This is one of the boldest claims in the book. Jacob's offspring will "lay the foundations of heaven", "make the earth firm" and "renew all the lights". Charles links it to 1:29, where the book speaks of the new creation. Isaiah 51:16 has God speak "so as to plant the heavens and found the earth", and 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1 speak of new heavens and a new earth.

a: The spirits of Mastema will not rule over you
t: Spirits over the nations, God over Israel
p: Jubilees teaches that evil spirits rule the nations but not Israel. Abraham applies it to Jacob.
b: Charles points to 15:31-32: God set spirits over every nation to lead them astray, but over Israel he set no angel or spirit, for he is their ruler. Here the spirits of Mastema (mänafəstä mästema) will not be able to turn Jacob from the Lord. Deuteronomy 32:8-9 has a related picture of the nations given to heavenly beings and Israel kept as the Lord's own portion.

a: May the Lord God be a father to you
p: Abraham prays that the Lord be Jacob's father and Jacob his firstborn, as Exodus 4:22 says of Israel.
b: Exodus 4:22: "Israel is my son, my firstborn." Abraham's blessing applies the title to Jacob himself. Jeremiah 31:9 uses it too: "For I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn." The New Testament gives "firstborn" to Christ (Colossians 1:15; Romans 8:29) and to the church (Hebrews 12:23).

a: his twelve sons
p: Genesis 25:13-16 lists Ishmael's twelve sons, "twelve chiefs".
b: Charles points to Genesis 25:13-15. The gathering of all of Abraham's sons and grandsons has no parallel in Genesis, which says only that Abraham gave gifts to his concubines' sons and sent them east (Genesis 25:6), as 20:11-12 here retells. Charles also thought the date ("seventh week") should be "sixth", so that some time passed before Abraham's death.

a: to keep the way of the Lord
p: Genesis 18:19 says God chose Abraham to teach his children to keep the way of the LORD.
b: Genesis 18:19 says God chose Abraham "so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the LORD's way by doing what is right and fair". Jubilees stages that command as a farewell speech to all his descendants, Ishmaelites and Keturah's sons included. The double command, to love one's neighbor and to do justice, echoes Leviticus 19:18 and Micah 6:8.

a: in every conflict
p: The Ge'ez says "in every war". Charles changed one letter to make it "among all people". See the variant.
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez has bäwsətä kʷəlu ḍäbʾ, "in every war". Charles read säbʾ, "people", instead, which gives "act the same way among all people". The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez and takes ḍäbʾ in its wider sense of strife: even in conflict, deal justly.

a: to circumcise their sons
p: Abraham commands all his descendants to circumcise, not only Isaac's line.
b: Ishmael was circumcised with Abraham (Genesis 17:23-26), and the command of Genesis 17:9-14 was for "your offspring after you". Charles notes that the Talmud (Sanhedrin 59b) discusses whether circumcision bound the sons of Ishmael and Keturah, and that Esau's descendants were held to be exempt because of Genesis 21:12. Jubilees, which elsewhere stresses circumcision on the eighth day for Israel (15:25-34), here charges all the family.

a: sexual sin and impurity
p: Two words that run through these testaments: zəmut, sexual sin, and rəkʷs, impurity.
b: The Ge'ez zəmut (Charles "fornication") covers sexual sin of every kind, like Greek porneia. Rəkʷs is impurity, the uncleanness that keeps one from God. Charles brackets the end of the verse as a copying repeat; VanderKam's text keeps it, and so does the Plain English Translation.

a: burn her with fire
t: Compared with the Bible: burning for sexual sin
p: The Torah prescribes burning only for a priest's daughter (Leviticus 21:9). Jubilees makes it general.
b: Charles notes that this rule does not match Leviticus or Deuteronomy, where the death penalty for adultery is by stoning (Deuteronomy 22:23-24) and burning is for a priest's daughter who sins sexually (Leviticus 21:9). It agrees instead with Judah's order to burn Tamar (Genesis 38:24), which Jubilees retells in chapter 41. This conflicts with the Torah's rules as written. The New Testament's answer to such cases is John 8:7-11, if that passage is accepted.

a: from the daughters of Canaan
p: The first of several warnings against marrying Canaanites, a main theme of these chapters.
b: Abraham told his servant not to take a wife for Isaac "from the daughters of the Canaanites" (Genesis 24:3), and Isaac told Jacob the same (Genesis 28:1). Jubilees makes it a command to all the family, repeats it to Jacob (22:20) and builds it into the Dinah story (chapter 30). The reason given is that Canaan's offspring will be uprooted (22:21; compare 10:29-34, where Canaan seizes Shem's land). For Jewish readers under Greek rule the warning spoke to marriage with their pagan neighbors.

a: the judgment of the giants and the judgment of Sodom
p: The giants and Sodom: the same pair of warnings as Jude 6-7 and 2 Peter 2:4-6.
b: Jubilees links the Flood's giants (5:1-11; 7:21-25) and Sodom (16:5-9) as two judgments for sexual sin and impurity. The New Testament pairs them the same way: Jude 6-7 places the angels who left their dwelling next to Sodom and Gomorrah, which "went after other flesh", and 2 Peter 2:4-6 has the angels, the Flood and Sodom. Many scholars think Jude and 2 Peter drew on this kind of Jewish teaching.

a: a thing to gloat over
p: The Ge'ez says your life will be "for boasting", that is, a thing others boast over. The Latin says "a hissing".
b: VanderKam's text has lätməkḥət, "for boasting". Charles's manuscripts read either "a threatening" or "a cause of boasting", and the Latin has "a hissing" (an object of scorn). Charles thinks the line is built on Jeremiah 29:18, where the exiles become "a curse, a shock, a thing to hiss at". See the variant.

a: there is no spirit in them at all
p: The words of the prophets and Psalms against idols, gathered into Abraham's speech.
b: Compare Jeremiah 10:14 ("there is no breath in them"), Habakkuk 2:19, and Psalm 115:4, "something human hands have made". "Do not serve them and do not bow down to them" is the second commandment (Exodus 20:5). Abraham, who burned the house of idols as a young man (12:12), now hands his fight on to his sons.

a: May he bless your bread and your water
p: Abraham uses the blessings of the law: Exodus 23:25 and Deuteronomy 7:13.
b: Charles points to Exodus 23:25, "he will bless your bread and your water", and Deuteronomy 7:13, "He will bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground... the calves of your herds and the lambs of your flocks." Abraham speaks the blessings Moses would give, a sign of the book's claim that the law was known before Sinai.

a: You will be a blessing on the earth
p: God's promise to Abram in Genesis 12:2-3, now said of his whole family.
b: Genesis 12:2 tells Abram, "And be a blessing!", and Genesis 12:3 says that all families of the earth will be blessed through him. Jubilees applies it to all his sons, then narrows it to Isaac (21:25) and Jacob (22:11-13).

a: from Paran to the entrance of Babylon
p: Ishmael's and Keturah's sons fill the desert east and south, from Paran to Babylon.
b: The Ge'ez spells Paran as farmon (Charles: "Pharmon"). Genesis 25:18 says Ishmael's sons lived "from Havilah to Shur", and Genesis 25:6 that Keturah's sons were sent "east, to the land of the East". Jubilees joins them into one people across the Arabian desert.

a: they were called Arabs and Ishmaelites
p: The Ge'ez calls the sons of Ishmael and Keturah "Arabs and Ishmaelites".
b: The Ge'ez has ʿäräb wäʾsəmaʿelawiyan. Genesis never uses the word "Arab" for Ishmael's line. The Latin version is different (see the variant). Galatians 4:25 links Hagar with "Mount Sinai in Arabia".

a: I do not know the day I will die
p: In Genesis 27:2 it is Isaac who says, "I do not know the day I will die."
b: Charles notes that these are Isaac's words in Genesis 27:2, here given to Abraham. He also shows that the Testament of Levi 9 has Isaac pass on to Levi the same priestly rules that Abraham gives Isaac in this chapter, and says "as Abraham also taught me". He judged that the Testament of Levi used Jubilees or a shared source, not the reverse.

a: I am a hundred and seventy-five years old
p: This is Abraham's age at death in Genesis 25:7. The book's dates here are muddled.
b: Genesis 25:7 gives Abraham "a hundred and seventy-five years". He says the same in 22:7, and 23:8 sums his life as three jubilees and four weeks. Charles notes that by the book's other dates Abraham should be about 174 here, and suggests "sixth" for "seventh" in 21:1.

a: no favoring of faces and no taking of gifts
p: From Deuteronomy 10:17. The New Testament repeats it often.
b: Deuteronomy 10:17: "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe." The Ge'ez has näśiʾä gäṣ, "lifting the face", the Hebrew idiom for favoritism. Paul says the same (Romans 2:11; Ephesians 6:9), and Peter at Cornelius's house (Acts 10:34). The point leads into the law about bribes for blood (21:19-20).
orig: ነሢአ ገጽ ወነሢአ ሕልያን (näśiʾä gäṣ wänäśiʾä ḥəlyan)

a: Do not eat any blood
p: Abraham repeats Noah's blood command (Genesis 9:4), which Jubilees treats as binding on all.
b: The command not to eat blood is given to Noah (Genesis 9:4; Jubilees 6:7-14; Jubilees 7:28-33), repeated in the law (Leviticus 7:26; Leviticus 17:10-14) and, in a form, by the Jerusalem council for Gentile believers (Acts 15:20, 29). For whether it still binds Christians, see the card at Leviticus 17.

a: a peace offering that will be accepted
p: Abraham teaches the peace-offering rules of Leviticus 3 centuries before Moses.
b: Charles points to Leviticus 3:7-10 and Leviticus 2:4 ("mixed with oil"). The site's Leviticus calls the offering "a soothing smell for the LORD" (Leviticus 1:9; Leviticus 3:16), the phrase Jubilees uses here. In Jubilees the patriarchs act as priests and pass the rules down; Moses later writes them down. The Latin leaves out "and the grain offering"; Charles first dropped it and then accepted it as genuine.

a: the fat of the peace offering
p: The Ge'ez says "sacrifice of salvation", from the Greek name for the peace offering.
b: Here the Ge'ez has mäśwaʿtä mädḫanit, "sacrifice of salvation (deliverance)". Greek Leviticus often calls the Hebrew peace offering (shelamim) thysia sōtēriou, "sacrifice of salvation", and the Ge'ez follows the Greek; in 21:7 it used another Greek name, "of peace" (sälam). Charles translated "thank offerings". It is one offering. The list of fat follows Leviticus 3:3-4. Charles corrected "rolled up" (ṭəblul) to "remove" from the Latin separa.

a: the food of the offering to the Lord
p: Leviticus 3:11 calls the burned fat "food, an offering by fire to the LORD".
b: The Ge'ez has ḫəbsətä ṣənḥäḥ, "the bread of the offering". Charles traces it to Leviticus 3:11. The Hebrew lechem means both bread and food. The prophets warned that God does not need food (Psalm 50:12-13); the phrase is a picture of fellowship at God's table.

a: Eat its meat on that day and on the next day
t: Compared with the Bible: two days
p: Leviticus allows two days for some peace offerings but one for the thank offering. Jubilees allows two.
b: Leviticus 7:15 says the thanks peace offering must be eaten on the day it is offered; vow and freewill offerings may be eaten the next day too (Leviticus 7:16-17; Leviticus 19:6). Jubilees, like Leviticus 19:6, gives two days for all and bans the third. Charles brackets "It has not been chosen" as a repeat. See the variant on the next clause.

a: in the words of Enoch and in the words of Noah
p: Abraham says he found these rules in the books of his forefathers. No such law book of Enoch survives.
b: Jubilees says Noah gave his books to Shem (10:14) and that Abram studied the books of his fathers (12:27). Charles notes that the Enoch books we have (1 Enoch) contain no laws of this kind, and thinks there was no ground for the claim. The claim matters for the book's argument: the laws of sacrifice are older than Moses, handed down in writing from the first fathers. Compare 7:38, where Noah cites Enoch.

a: the covenant of salt
p: The Ge'ez says "covenant of salt", as Numbers 18:19 does. Leviticus 2:13 has "salt of the covenant".
b: VanderKam's text and Charles's manuscripts read kidanä ḍew, "the covenant of salt". Charles changed it to "salt of the covenant" to match Leviticus 2:13, "Do not leave the salt of your God's covenant out of your grain offering." The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez, which matches Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5. Salt, which does not spoil, stood for a covenant that lasts. Jesus says, "everyone will be salted with fire" (Mark 9:49).

a: cypress, defran, sagad, pine, fir, cedar, savin, palm, olive, myrtle, laurel, the qedar whose name is arbat, and balsam
p: A list of evergreen woods for the altar fire. Several names are Greek, and some are uncertain.
b: The Ge'ez names are qep̣arson, defran, sogad, säṭärobilon, p̣iṭin, qedron, burati, tanak, ʿəḍä zäyt, mərsəne, dəfn, qedar "whose name is arbat", and besm. Several are Greek words: kyparissos (cypress), strobilos (pine), pitys, kedros (cedar), myrsinē (myrtle), daphnē (laurel). The Plain English Translation gives the Greek-based names their plain sense, renders mərsəne "myrtle" from the Greek myrsinē, and leaves defran, sagad and the qedar as they stand. Charles's English differs: he has "myrrh" for mərsəne, and he takes qedar as a corruption of the Greek kitrion and renders "citron, juniper". His identifications of défran (perhaps a kind of fir) and sagad (not the almond, since all the trees are evergreen) are suggestions. Charles compares a list of fourteen evergreens in the Greek farming book Geoponica. The Testament of Levi 9 speaks of "twelve trees always in leaf" taught by Abraham, and 1 Enoch 3 of fourteen evergreen trees.

a: whole and new growth
p: Jubilees rules on the quality of altar wood. Later rabbis had their own, different rules.
b: The Torah only says the priests are to put wood on the altar (Leviticus 1:7; Leviticus 6:12). Charles notes that rabbinic law has nothing like this rule, and that the Mishnah (Tamid 2:3) allows all kinds of wood except olive and vine. Jubilees, by contrast, lists olive among the approved woods. The rule shows the priestly concerns of the book: even the wood must be fit for God.

a: for their fragrance is distinct
p: The Ge'ez says the smell of these woods goes up to heaven. Charles added a "not" and changed the sense.
b: VanderKam's text reads ʾəsmä mäʿazahu fəloṭ wäyäʿärg, "for its fragrance is distinct and goes up". Charles took fəloṭ as "dispersed" and, following Littmann, inserted a negative: other woods' fragrance "goes not up". His English (1913) keeps the negative. The Ge'ez as it stands makes good sense: the listed woods are set apart, and their smell rises to God. See the variant.

a: Wash yourself with water
p: The priests' washing of Exodus 30:19-21, here taught by Abraham to Isaac.
b: Exodus 30:20: "Before they enter the tent of meeting they must wash with water, or they will die. The same holds when they come near the altar." Jubilees adds washing again after the offering. Charles shows that the Testament of Levi 9 repeats this rule "almost word for word".

a: Cover it with dirt
p: From Leviticus 17:13: the blood of game must be covered with dirt.
b: The site's Leviticus: "who hunts down a wild animal or a bird that may be eaten must pour out its blood and cover it with dirt" (Leviticus 17:13). Jubilees extends the care for blood to the priest's body and clothes.

a: for blood is the life
p: The Ge'ez says "blood is the soul" (näfs), the word for life, breath and soul.
b: The Ge'ez däm näfs yəʾti, "blood, it is soul", follows Deuteronomy 12:23, "the blood is the life", and Leviticus 17:11, 14. Ge'ez näfs, like Hebrew nefesh, means life, self or soul. The Plain English Translation uses "life", as the site's Deuteronomy does.

a: it is blood that is shed that makes the earth sin
p: From Numbers 35:33: only the killer's blood can make the land clean again.
b: Numbers 35:33: "Blood pollutes the land. No atonement can be made for the land for the blood shed on it, except by the blood of the one who shed it." Charles says "makes the earth sin" goes back to the Hebrew "pollutes", and points to 7:33. Numbers 35:31 also forbids taking a ransom for a murderer's life, the "gift" Abraham forbids here.

a: Blood for blood
p: The Ge'ez says blood for blood "will be accepted". Charles changed it to "that you may be accepted".
b: VanderKam's text has dämä bädäm wäyśäṭäw, "blood for blood, and it will be accepted". Charles's manuscripts differ ("it will be accepted", "it will not be accepted", "he will accept you"), and he printed an emended "that thou mayest be accepted". The next clause, wäykäwn ʿuqabehu läśänay, Charles took as "for He is the defence of the good"; it can also mean "keeping it will be for good". The Plain English Translation follows the second sense.

a: a sin that leads to death
p: Charles links the phrase to Numbers 18:22 and 1 John 5:16.
b: The Ge'ez səḥtätä lämot is "an error unto death". Charles compares Numbers 18:22, where Israelites who come near the tent "will bear sin and die", and 1 John 5:16, "There is sin headed toward death." Charles points ahead to 33:18. Charles brackets "he will hide his face from you" as an addition that spoils the poetry; VanderKam's text has it.

a: the plant of righteousness
p: Israel as a righteous plant, a picture shared with 1 Enoch and Isaiah.
b: The Ge'ez täklä ṣədq, "the plant of righteousness", is the same phrase as 1 Enoch 10:16 and 1 Enoch 93:2-10, where it stands for the chosen line of Abraham and Israel. Charles points to 16:26. Isaiah calls the restored people "Oaks of Righteousness, the LORD's planting" (Isaiah 61:3).

a: in the second year, the year in which Abraham died
p: Charles thought every number in this date was wrong.
b: Charles notes that the dates in this verse add up to a year far later than Abraham's death by the book's other figures, and offers "the sixth week of the forty-second jubilee, the seventh year". VanderKam's Ge'ez text reads "the first week of the forty-fourth jubilee, the second year", and the Plain English Translation keeps it. What matters to the story is that Abraham dies right after a Feast of Weeks.
orig: በሱባዔ ቀዳሚ በዘ አርብዓ ወአርባዕ ኢዮቤልዉ (bäsubaʿe qädami bäzä ʾärbəʿa wäʾärbaʿ ʾiyobelwu)

a: the Feast of Weeks, which is the feast of the first fruits of the harvest
p: The Feast of Weeks is the book's covenant festival. Abraham dies just after keeping it with his sons.
b: Exodus 34:22 links the Feast of Weeks with "the first crops of the wheat harvest". Jubilees teaches that it was kept in heaven and first given to Noah as a yearly renewal of the covenant (6:17-22), and that Abraham kept it (15:1-2). So the family gathers on the covenant feast, Ishmael included, and Abraham passes the blessing to Jacob. Christians later received the Spirit at this feast, Pentecost (Acts 2:1).

a: new cakes from the new grain
p: Rebekah's cakes are first fruits: the new grain, offered and eaten at the Feast of Weeks.
b: The Ge'ez dafnətä ḥädasä ʾəmsərnay ḥädis is "new cakes from new wheat". Leviticus 23:16-17 commands a new grain offering at the Feast of Weeks, two loaves from the new grain. Jubilees turns that into a family meal: Rebekah sends the first-fruit bread with Jacob, so that Abraham may bless God before he dies.
orig: ዳፍንተ ሐዳሰ እምስርናይ ሐዲስ (dafnətä ḥädasä ʾəmsərnay ḥädis)

a: his grandfather Abraham
p: The Ge'ez says "his father", as Charles prints. Abraham is Jacob's grandfather, so the English says so.
b: The Ge'ez ʾäbuhu is "his father". In Hebrew and Ge'ez "father" can mean any forefather, as in "Abraham our father" (James 2:21). The book itself calls Abraham "his father's father" a few verses later (22:26; 23:2).

a: all the rich things of the earth
p: The Ge'ez says "the fat of the earth", a Hebrew way of saying its richest food.
b: The Ge'ez səbḥä mədr is "the fat of the earth", the same word as the fat of the offerings (21:7-8). Isaac's blessing in Genesis 27:28 asks for "some of the richness of the earth". Abraham praises God for food and for the meal that lets people bless him. Charles notes that "Creator of all" (22:4) is a favorite title in this book, and compares Sirach 24:8 and 2 Maccabees 1:24.

a: all my days have been peace for me
p: God promised Abram a peaceful death at a good old age (Genesis 15:15). Abraham says it came true.
b: In Genesis 15:15, God told Abram, "you yourself will go in peace to your fathers; you will be buried at a good old age." Abraham's prayer thanks God for exactly that. Genesis 25:8 says he "died at a good old age, old and satisfied". Compare Simeon's prayer, "now you are setting your slave free to go in peace" (Luke 2:29).

a: your chosen people and your inheritance
p: Israel as God's inheritance is the language of Deuteronomy 4:20 and Deuteronomy 32:9.
b: Charles points to Deuteronomy 4:20 and to verses 10, 15 and 29 of this chapter, where the phrase repeats. The idea that Israel is the Lord's own share among the nations comes from Deuteronomy 32:9. Abraham prays it over the family, the Ishmaelites present, but the blessing goes to Jacob.

a: May nations serve you
t: Isaac's blessing, first said by Abraham
p: The words of Genesis 27:29, Isaac's blessing of Jacob, said here first by Abraham.
b: Genesis 27:29: "May peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you." Charles notes that Abraham's blessing borrows it. In Jubilees, Isaac's later blessing (26:23-24) only repeats what Abraham already gave. Rebekah's plan in Genesis 27 then carries out Abraham's will, which is how Jubilees reads that troubling story.

a: and all his sons, to the Lord Most High
t: "His sons, to the Lord Most High"
p: Charles printed "all the sons of God Most High". VanderKam's Ge'ez has "his sons".
b: VanderKam's text reads wäkʷlomu wəludu läʾgəziʾäbḥer ləʿul, "and all his sons, to the Lord Most High". Charles gave "all the sons of God Most High" with the alternative "his sons unto the God Most High", and compared Genesis 14:19, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High". On Israel as sons of God, he points to his 1:24, which is 1:25 in VanderKam's numbering used here.
orig: ወኵሎሙ ውሉዱ ለእግዚአብሔር ልዑል (wäkʷlomu wəludu läʾgəziʾäbḥer ləʿul)

a: rule over all the offspring of Seth
p: Seth's offspring means all humankind. The phrase also appears in Balaam's oracle.
b: Since all people after the Flood come from Seth through Noah, "all the offspring of Seth" means all humanity. Charles notes that the phrase is also in Numbers 24:17, where Balaam's star from Jacob crushes "all the sons of Sheth"; he takes Sheth there as a different word, "tumult". Jubilees reads it as the patriarch's name. The Latin has "rule" as a command; the Ge'ez has "ruling".

a: May they rest on the holy head of your offspring
p: From Jacob's blessing of Joseph, "May they rest on the head of Joseph" (Genesis 49:26).
b: Genesis 49:26: "The blessings of your father are stronger... May they rest on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the one set apart from his brothers." Charles notes the link and that "holy head" may reflect the word nazir, "set apart" (compare Numbers 6:9).

a: every wrong you did without knowing it
p: Abraham prays that Jacob be forgiven sins done without knowing, the kind the law could atone for.
b: The Ge'ez zäbä ʾiyaʾməro gegaykä is "which you sinned in not knowing". The law of Leviticus 4-5 and Numbers 15:22-29 provides offerings for sins done unknowingly, but not for sins "with a high hand" (Numbers 15:30). Charles notes the Latin reads "He may forgive" for "you may be forgiven", and adds "your" and "and" from it.

a: Separate yourself from the nations
p: The strongest call in the book to keep apart from Gentiles, even at the table.
b: Charles saw here the separatism of Judaism in the 100s BC, when the Greek king Antiochus IV tried to make Jews eat unclean food (1 Maccabees 1:47-48, 62-63; 2 Maccabees 6:18-21). A Jew could not share a Gentile meal, since the meat might be unclean or offered to idols. Isaiah 52:11 says "Touch nothing unclean." The New Testament shows the same rule at Peter's visit to Cornelius (Acts 10:28; Acts 11:3) and the quarrel at Antioch (Galatians 2:12), where Paul argues that Jews and Gentiles in Christ may eat together.
r: Isaiah 52:11; Acts 10:28; Acts 11:3; Galatians 2:11-14; 2 Corinthians 6:17; Daniel 1:8

a: They offer their sacrifices to the dead
p: Meals and offerings for the dead at graves, a practice the Bible also condemns.
b: Charles points to Deuteronomy 26:14 ("I have not given any of it for the dead"), Psalm 106:28 ("ate the sacrifices of the dead"), Sirach 30:18-19 and Tobit 4:17. Meals were set out at graves and eaten there, which is "eating among the graves". "They bow down to demons" echoes Deuteronomy 32:17 and Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:20: "what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God."
r: Deuteronomy 26:14; Psalm 106:28; Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20; Isaiah 65:4; Tobit 4:17

a: saying to wood, 'You are my God,'
p: From Jeremiah 2:27, the prophet's mockery of those who pray to wood and stone.
b: The site's Jeremiah: "They say to a piece of wood, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave birth to us'" (Jeremiah 2:27). Jubilees changes the titles to "my God", "my Lord" and "my rescuer". "They have no heart" at the end Charles brackets as a repeat of the verse's start; VanderKam's text has it.

a: because of Ham's wrong, Canaan went astray
t: Compared with the Bible: the curse of Canaan
p: Jubilees blames Canaan's fate on Ham and on Canaan's own sin, and says none of his line will be saved.
b: Genesis 9:25 curses Canaan for Ham's act. Jubilees adds Canaan's own wrong: he seized land given to Shem (10:29-34). It then says no one born from Canaan will be saved "on the day of judgment". This goes beyond the Bible, and conflicts with it in spirit: Rahab of Jericho, a Canaanite, is saved and enters the line of David (Joshua 6:25; Matthew 1:5), and Jesus heals the daughter of a Canaanite woman (Matthew 15:22-28). The curse of Ham has been badly misused to defend slavery; the Bible's curse names Canaan, not Ham's other sons.

a: they will go down to Sheol
t: Sheol and the place of judgment
p: Idol worshipers go down to Sheol, the world of the dead, and to a place of judgment.
b: The Ge'ez uses siʾol, borrowed from the Hebrew Sheol. Charles compares 7:29, where the same two phrases occur, and 1 Enoch 103:7-8, where the souls of sinners go down to Sheol and suffer there. So in Jubilees, Sheol is not only the shadowy grave of the older books (Psalm 6:5) but already a place of punishment. VanderKam's Ge'ez has "the hated ones" (ṣəluʾan); Charles emended it to "the profane".

a: This house I have built for myself
p: Abraham gives his house to Jacob. Jacob "will build my house": a family, and perhaps a temple.
b: In Hebrew "house" means both a building and a family line, as in God's promise to build David a house (2 Samuel 7:11-16). Abraham's house in Hebron passes to Jacob, and Jacob "will build my house and set up my name before God". Jubilees later has Jacob give Levi the books and tells of the house of Levi (45:16). Charles brackets the first "It is given to you and to your offspring forever" as a copying repeat; VanderKam's text has it twice.

a: Jacob slept in the arms of Abraham
p: Jacob sleeps "in Abraham's bosom", as the poor man Lazarus rests in Abraham's arms in Luke 16:22.
b: The Ge'ez ḥəḍnä ʾäbrəham is "the bosom (lap) of Abraham". In Jesus' parable, the poor man is carried "to Abraham's embrace" (Luke 16:22-23), often called "Abraham's bosom". Jubilees uses the picture of a child and a grandfather on one bed. Whether Jesus' hearers knew this scene cannot be shown, but the image of rest with Abraham was common.

a: who brought me out of Ur of the Chaldeans
p: From Genesis 15:7: "I am the LORD, who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land."
b: Abraham repeats God's own words to him (Genesis 15:7; compare Nehemiah 9:7). Charles thought the verse might be added later, since it is meant to bless Jacob but never names him; he also notes that the last words can mean "blessed be the Most High forever" or "that he may be blessed forever".

a: may your kindness and your mercy be lifted over him
p: Halfway through, Abraham stops speaking to Jacob and prays to God for him.
b: The verse begins addressing Jacob ("My son") but goes on with "your kindness and your mercy", meaning God's; the Plain English Translation adds "Lord," to show the turn. Charles notes that two of his manuscripts read "rejoice" as third person, making it "over whom my heart and my love rejoice". "Lifted over him" may echo the priestly blessing, "May the LORD lift up his face toward you" (Numbers 6:26).

a: He laid two of Jacob's fingers on his eyes
p: Abraham uses Jacob's hand to close his own eyes, the duty of a son at death.
b: Charles compares Genesis 46:4, where God promises Jacob, "Joseph will lay his hand on your eyes." Here Abraham places Jacob's fingers on his own eyes, making his grandson the one who performs the last act. "Stretched out his feet" differs from Genesis 49:33, where Jacob "gathered his feet into the bed". Charles notes the Syriac and Ethiopic versions of Genesis 49:33 also have "stretched out".

a: slept the sleep of eternity
p: The Ge'ez nəwamä zäläʿaläm is "the sleep that is forever", a phrase from Jeremiah.
b: Charles points to Jeremiah 51:39, 57, where Babylon's leaders "sleep an endless sleep and not wake up". The New Testament uses sleep for the death of believers, who will wake (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14; John 11:11). In this book the phrase does not settle what happens after death; see 23:31.

a: he was gathered to his fathers
p: Genesis 25:8 says Abraham "was gathered to his people". Jubilees has "to his fathers".
b: Charles notes that "gathered to his fathers" first occurs in Judges 2:10, while Genesis 25:8 has "to his people". Both speak of joining the ancestors in death.

a: cold as ice
t: Compared with the Bible: Abraham's death
p: Genesis gives Abraham's death in one verse. Jubilees tells it as a scene, with Jacob in his arms.
b: Genesis 25:8: "Then Abraham breathed his last and died at a good old age, old and satisfied, and he was gathered to his people." Jubilees adds the last night, the boy who does not know, the cold body, the lamp and the weeping house. It goes beyond the Bible, but its picture of a calm death after blessing the next generation follows Jacob's own death in Genesis 49:33.

a: Isaac fell on his father's face
p: The words of Genesis 50:1, Joseph at Jacob's death, used here of Isaac.
b: Genesis 50:1: "Joseph fell upon his father's face. He wept over him and kissed him." Charles notes the source.

a: His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him
p: From Genesis 25:9: the two brothers bury their father together.
b: Genesis 25:9: "His sons Isaac and Ishmael laid him to rest in the cave of Machpelah." Jubilees adds forty days of mourning by the whole family, Keturah's sons too. Forty days are the days of embalming Jacob in Genesis 50:3; Israel mourned Moses thirty days (Deuteronomy 34:8).

a: three jubilees and four weeks of years
p: A hundred and seventy-five is 147 + 28: three jubilees and four weeks of years.
b: The book counts Abraham's life its own way: three jubilees (3 x 49 = 147) and four weeks of years (28). The total matches Genesis 25:7. The point that follows (23:9-10) is that he did not reach four jubilees.

a: nineteen jubilees
p: Nineteen jubilees is 931 years, close to Adam's 930 (Genesis 5:5).
b: Nineteen times forty-nine is 931. Genesis gives Adam 930 years and Methuselah 969 (Genesis 5:5, 27). Jubilees says Adam died seventy years short of a thousand because of his sin (4:30), so "nineteen jubilees" is a round figure for the first fathers. After the Flood, life spans fall, which the book blames on trouble and wickedness. Charles notes the Latin is simpler here: "to grow old more quickly and the days of their life to be lessened."

a: Abraham was perfect in all his deeds with the Lord
t: Compared with the Bible: was Abraham perfect?
p: Jubilees calls Abraham perfect. Genesis shows his faith and his failures.
b: Genesis 17:1 tells Abram, "Go about your life in my sight, and be whole", and Genesis 26:5 says he kept God's commands. But Genesis also tells of his lies about Sarah (Genesis 12:11-20; Genesis 20:1-13) and his doubt (Genesis 17:17). Jubilees retold those scenes gently. It calls him "perfect", yet even he grew old early "in the face of evil", that is, because of the evil of his age. Paul's view is that Abraham was counted righteous by faith, not by perfect deeds (Romans 4:2-5). For the faith-and-works question, see the card at Romans 4.

a: the day of the great judgment
t: The day of the great judgment
p: The book looks ahead to a final judgment. Charles asks whether it comes before or after the age of blessing.
b: The Ge'ez ʿəlätä däyn ʿäbay is "the day of the great judgment", a phrase also in 1 Enoch 10:6 and 1 Enoch 22:11. Charles notes that here the judgment seems to come before the time of blessing in 23:27-31, but argues that the book's gradual kingdom makes more sense with the judgment at its end. Charles also says the Latin leaves out the last clause, "and all their knowledge will vanish", which he calls a repeat.

a: a jubilee and a half of years
p: A jubilee and a half is about seventy-four years, close to Psalm 90:10's "seventy, or eighty for the strong".
b: Charles points to Psalm 90:10: "The days of our years add up to seventy, or eighty for the strong. What they boast of is hard work and grief." Jubilees quotes the same psalm in 23:15. The book reads the psalm as a sign of decline from the long lives of the first fathers.

a: sickness and ruin, snow, hail and frost, fever, chills and numbness
p: Some of these Ge'ez words occur nowhere else, so the English follows Charles and the Latin.
b: The Ge'ez list runs däwe, gäbäṭbaṭ, ʾäsḥätya, bäräd, ḥämäda, näbärṣaw, säkäḥkaḥ, säʿozaz, ʿäbar, mot, mäṭbaḥt and ḍiwawe. Charles says the words he renders "fever and chills" follow the Latin, since the Ethiopic words occur only here. He did not tie this list to particular events: he headed 23:18-24 "The Messianic woes", and saw the vision turn to "a definite description of the Maccabean times" at 23:16 and 23:19.
orig: ደዌ ወኵሉ ኵነኔ እኩይ ዘከማሁ ዝንቱ ምስለ ዝንቱ ደዌ ወገበጥባጥ ወአስሐትያ ወበረድ ወሐመዳ ወነበርጻው ወሰከሕካሕ ወሰዖዛዝ ወዐባር ወሞት ወመጥባሕት ወፂዋዌ (däwe wäkʷlu kʷənäne ʾəkuy zäkämahu zəntu məslä zəntu däwe wägäbäṭbaṭ wäʾäsḥätya wäbäräd wäḥämäda wänäbärṣaw wäsäkäḥkaḥ wäsäʿozaz wäʿäbar wämot wämäṭbaḥt wäḍiwawe)

a: the sons will accuse their fathers and their elders
t: Who are the sons who accuse?
p: Charles saw here the rise of the Hasideans, the pious party of the Maccabean age.
b: Charles read 23:16-31 as history written as prophecy. The "sons" who accuse their fathers and elders are the Hasideans (1 Maccabees 2:42), who challenged the leaders of Judaism; the armed struggle of 23:20 is Judas Maccabeus fighting the Hellenizing Jews; and the turmoil of 23:21-23 is the civil strife after 162 BC. He compared the lambs who open their eyes in 1 Enoch 90:6-7, and noted that W. Bousset had already linked the chapter to the Maccabean movement. Charles himself took parts of the passage as a general picture: he headed 23:18-24 "The Messianic woes". See the chapter page.

a: without turning aside to the left or to the right
t: Not to the right or the left
p: Deuteronomy's phrase for keeping the law exactly (Deuteronomy 5:32; Deuteronomy 28:14).
b: Charles points to Deuteronomy 5:32-33 and Deuteronomy 28:13-14, and to 1 Maccabees 2:22, where Mattathias refuses "to go aside from our worship to the right hand or the left". He took that as a sign that the phrase was a watchword of the Maccabean revolt.

a: There will be no seed of the vine and no oil
t: The earth suffers for human sin
p: As in Hosea 4:3: the land mourns, and animals, birds and fish waste away because of sin.
b: Charles points to Hosea 4:3, Ezekiel 38:20 and Zephaniah 1:3, where the animals, birds and fish perish with sinful people. The idea that the earth suffers for human sin goes back to Genesis 3:17 and is taken up in Romans 8:20-22, where creation groans and waits for freedom.

a: feast and month, Sabbath and jubilee
p: The sin of the last generation is that they forget the feasts, months, Sabbaths and jubilees.
b: For Jubilees the calendar is part of the covenant: the 364-day year was written on the heavenly tablets (6:23-38), and Israel would one day forget it and keep the wrong days (6:34-38). Here the forgetting is the cause of strife. Charles saw the apostate Jews of the Maccabean age, who gave up the Sabbath and the feasts (1 Maccabees 1:43-45). For whether Christians must keep a set calendar, see the card on 1 Enoch 72-82 and the Sabbath cards.

a: They will rise up with swords and with fighting
t: An armed return to the law
p: Those who return to the way try to force others back by war. Charles saw the Maccabees here.
b: Charles took this as the efforts of Judas Maccabeus to force apostate Jews back to Judaism, and noted that in 162 BC the Syrian king allowed the Jews to live by their laws (1 Maccabees 6:55-62). After that the fight was between Jewish parties. The Latin adds "with bows" before "swords" (see the variant). The book does not praise the bloodshed: they "will not turn back until much blood has been shed".

a: They will name the great name
p: They swear by God's name, "but not in truth". Charles saw the Hellenizing priests of the 160s BC.
b: To "name the name" is to call on God or swear by him (Isaiah 48:1; compare 2 Timothy 2:19). Charles thought the target was the Hellenizing party under the high priest Alcimus, who held the Temple and, in this writer's view, defiled the holiest place. Charles notes "great name" in Joshua 7:9.

a: the sinners of the nations
p: Gentiles and sinners were almost one word to this writer, as Paul's "sinners from the Gentiles" shows.
b: The Ge'ez ḫaṭiʾanihomu läʾäḥzab is "their sinners of the nations". Charles says that to the writer "Gentiles" and "sinners" were practically the same, and compares Galatians 2:15, "By nature we are Jews, and not sinners from the Gentiles." In 23:24 the Ge'ez puts the two words side by side ("the sinners, the nations"), which Charles took as a translator's slip for "the sinners of the nations". He also links the cruel invader to Jeremiah 6:23.

a: no one to gather the dead and no one to bury them
p: From Jeremiah 8:2: the bones of the people lie ungathered.
b: Charles points to Jeremiah 8:2: "The bones will not be gathered up or buried." Psalm 79:3 laments the same: "there was nobody to bury them."

a: A child of three weeks of years will look old
t: Three weeks, or three weeks of years?
p: In Jubilees a "week" usually means seven years, so the Plain English Translation reads "three weeks of years": a youth of twenty-one.
b: The Ge'ez ḥəḍan wäldä śälästu subaʿe is "a child, a son of three weeks". Charles translated "a child of three weeks". But this book almost always uses subaʿe for a week of years, and the Plain English Translation follows that use here, which makes the "child" a youth of twenty-one, gray like a man of a hundred. Read as days, it is a baby three weeks old. Charles compares Hesiod's iron age, when children are born with gray temples, and the Sibylline Oracles 2:155.
orig: ሕፃን ወልደ ሠለስቱ ሱባዔ (ḥəḍan wäldä śälästu subaʿe)

a: the children will begin to study the laws
t: The turning point: study of the law
p: The return begins with the young studying the law. Then life spans grow again.
b: This is the turning point of the vision. Charles saw in it a renewed study of the law that would bring a gradual change for the better, with a matching renewal of heaven and earth (1:29; Isaiah 65:17). Deuteronomy 30:1-6 also promises restoration when Israel turns back to the law, and 1:23-25 of this book promises a new heart.

a: until their days come near a thousand years
p: In the age of renewal, people will live close to a thousand years, as before the Flood.
b: Charles says that in the messianic kingdom people reach the age God first intended; Adam fell short of a thousand because of sin (4:29-30). Isaiah 65:20-22 promises that whoever dies at a hundred will die young, and "like the lifetime of a tree will be the lifetime of my people". Revelation 20:4-6 speaks of a thousand-year reign, a different idea that some readers link with this one.

a: no one who has had his fill of days
p: Charles added "not" to this line. The Ge'ez makes good sense without it.
b: VanderKam's text reads wäʾälbo zäyṣägb mäwaʿlä, "and there is no one who is full of days". To be "full of days" is to have reached a ripe old age (Genesis 25:8; Genesis 35:29). Charles inserted a negative, "nor one who is not satisfied with his days", from Isaiah 65:20 ("an old man who does not fill out his days"). The Ge'ez as it stands says there will be no worn-out old people, which fits "all of them will be infants and children".

a: There will be no satan and no evil one to destroy
p: Here Jubilees uses the Ge'ez word säyṭan, 'satan', as a common noun: no adversary at all.
b: The Ge'ez mänähi säyṭanä means "any satan" or "any adversary". In this book the word appears in passages about peace with no accuser: the days of Joseph (46:2) and the Sabbath law (50:5). Charles compares the Testament of Moses 10:1. Revelation 20:2-3 and Revelation 20:10 end the devil's power. The Plain English Translation writes "satan" in lowercase here, since it is a common noun, "adversary", in a pair with "evil one", and keeps "Mastema" for Mastema.

a: They will rise up and see great peace
p: Does "they will rise up" mean resurrection? Charles weighed it and thought not: the servants are healed and stand up strong.
b: The Ge'ez wäytənäśʾu means "they will rise, get up". Charles weighed two readings. If the verse means that the righteous are raised to share in the kingdom, then this book would separate the resurrection from the final judgment, which comes only at the kingdom's close. But he judged that the words "apparently" do not refer to resurrection: when the Lord heals his servants (compare Revelation 22:2, and 23:29 here, "days of blessing and healing") they become strong. See 23:31 and the chapter page.

a: Their bones will rest in the earth, and their spirits will have much joy
t: Bones at rest, spirits in joy
p: The key verse on the afterlife in Jubilees. Charles read it as no bodily resurrection, but a joyful life of the spirit.
b: Charles wrote: "After death there is no resurrection of the body, but a blessed immortality awaiting the spirit", and matched it with 1 Enoch 91-104 (for example 1 Enoch 103:3-4). In his introduction he calls this the earliest attested instance of that hope in the last two centuries BC. On that reading the book, unlike Daniel 12:2, expects the righteous dead to live on as spirits while their bones stay in the ground. The text itself says only that bones rest and spirits rejoice. For how the churches read the state of the dead, see the cards at Philippians 1 and 1 Enoch 102.

a: shows mercy to hundreds and to thousands, and to all who love him
p: From the Ten Commandments: "I show loyal love to thousands, for those who love me" (Exodus 20:6).
b: The end of the vision returns to Exodus 20:6 and Deuteronomy 7:9, the promise of God's faithfulness to those who love him. The Ge'ez adds "hundreds". Charles notes that one manuscript reads "of all who love him".

a: And you, Moses, write down these words
p: The angel turns to Moses: the whole vision is part of what he is told to write on the mountain.
b: The book reminds the reader of its frame (1:1-7, 1:26-29): the angel of the presence dictates to Moses on Sinai. The vision of 23:9-31 is copied from the heavenly tablets "for a testimony" (səmʿ, the book's word for a witness kept in writing). Revelation 1:11 and Revelation 21:5 also have a seer told to write what he sees.
